topic.title: Analysing experimental data: accuracy, reliability, validity, anomalies and graphs
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 7 is a quarter of the award. Every Booklet A task processes its own readings (a mean, a worked-out column, a rate or a speed to the stated places) and most set a graph; every Booklet B paper has a five-mark graph (scale, label, points, line) and often a gradient with its unit, a total read from a curve or an anomaly left out of a mean.
mustMemorise: Record readings to the places the table asks for; the unit goes in the heading, quantity / unit
Leave an anomalous reading out of the mean, and divide by the number of readings kept
Extension = stretched length − unstretched length; rate = 1 ÷ time; average speed = distance ÷ time
A scale must be linear and cover at least half of each axis; each axis label is the column heading
Physics and Chemistry: one straight line or smooth curve of best fit; Biology: point to point only when the question says so
The total volume of gas is the level part of the curve, never the readings added up
Gradient = rise ÷ run from a large triangle; its unit is the y unit per x unit
The gradient of force against extension is the spring constant k; of voltage against current, the resistance R
notOnThisSpec: Error bars, uncertainty and the uncertainty of a gradient
Lines of best fit worked out by calculation (least squares) rather than drawn by eye

note.subject: science

mustKnow: gradient = rise ÷ run, in y-axis unit per x-axis unit
F = ke, so k is the gradient of force against extension
R = V ÷ I, so R is the gradient of voltage against current

Lines of best fit found by calculation

mustBeAbleTo: Record readings to the stated places, with units in the headings and a mean column
Spot an anomalous reading, leave it out and average the rest with the sum in brackets
Work out a new column: extension by subtracting, rate as 1 ÷ time, speed as distance ÷ time
Choose a linear scale that fills at least half of each axis, and label each axis quantity / unit
Plot to within half a small square and draw the right line: best fit in Physics and Chemistry, point to point in Biology when asked
Read a total from the level part of a curve and the time the reaction stopped
Find a gradient from a large triangle, give its unit and say what it means
Tell accuracy, reliability and validity apart and say what improves each
sheet.howExamined: Booklet A is three practical tasks done in school, 15 marks each; after the readings come the processing marks: a mean, a worked-out column, a rate or a speed to the stated places, and often a graph of a printed data set. Booklet B is three 30-minute written papers of 35 marks: nearly every paper has a five-mark graph (the scale, the label with its unit, the points and the line), and many add a gradient with its unit, a total read from a curve, a value read from the line or an anomaly to leave out before averaging.
traps: The x-axis label left off, and the total volume of gas found by adding every reading in the table instead of reading the level part of the curve (Summer 2025 Booklet B Chemistry Higher Q2 and Foundation Q2)
An anomalous reading kept in the average, losing both marks (Summer 2024 Booklet B Physics Higher Q2 and Foundation Q4)
A non-linear scale on a circuit graph, and the voltmeter placed in series (Summer 2024 Booklet B Physics Higher Q3)
An axis without its label, a scale whose equal distances do not mean equal steps, and a curve ruled from point to point (Summer 2023 Booklet B Physics Higher Q4)
The gradient worked out, but its unit wrong (Summer 2025 Booklet B Physics Higher Q3)
Concentration written on the axis without its unit (Summer 2023 Booklet B Chemistry Higher Q3)
Rates not recorded to the four decimal places asked for (Summer 2023 Booklet A Chemistry Higher Q1)
A ruled straight line or point-to-point line where a curve was needed, or a bar chart drawn instead (Summer 2023 Booklet B Chemistry Foundation Q3)
Not saying the distance and time are measured before the speed is calculated, and ignoring the bold instruction to give 1 decimal place (Summer 2023 Booklet B Physics Higher Q3)
Readings not to the decimal places asked, V ÷ I worked wrongly on the calculator, and voltage given as the independent variable when the current was set (Summer 2023 Booklet A Physics Foundation Q1)
Hooke's law not recalled, and very few using the word subtract to find an extension (Summer 2024 Booklet B Physics Foundation Q1)
The dependent variable not named exactly as the compressed length, and the unit of k not known (Summer 2024 Booklet B Physics Higher Q4)
The unit left out of the axis label; the column heading should be the axis label word for word (Summer 2025 Booklet A Physics Foundation Q1)

noteBlocks.lede: This lesson is about turning readings into results: a table to the right places, a mean without the odd reading, a worked-out column, and a graph with the right scale, line and gradient. It prepares you for the processing in your Booklet A tasks and the graph questions of Booklet B. The practical itself you do by hand, in school.
can: Record readings to the stated places, find a mean without the anomaly and work out a new column
Choose a scale, label the axes, plot the points and draw the right line or curve
Read a total and a gradient from a graph, with the gradient's unit and meaning

noteBlocks.md: A page of readings means little until it is processed. The table, the mean, the graph and the gradient are where most of the marks sit, and each follows a few fixed habits you can practise until they are automatic.

noteBlocks.text: The table is where the marks start

noteBlocks.md: Record each reading to the places the table asks for, with the unit in the heading and numbers only in the cells. Repeats get their own columns, then a mean column. A count is discrete, a whole number; a length, a time or a temperature is continuous and can take any value in between.

noteBlocks.stem: A ball rolls 80 cm between the markers of a runway raised 6 cm. Its two timings are 1.62 s and 1.58 s. Record them, find the mean time and the average speed to 1 decimal place.

steps.working: Time 1 = 1.62 s; time 2 = 1.58 s
steps.decision: Both to 0.01 s, the stopwatch's step, with s in the column heading.
Brackets round the sum, so the calculator adds before it divides.

steps.working: Average speed = distance ÷ time = 80 ÷ 1.60 = 50.0 cm/s
steps.decision: To 1 decimal place the zero is written: 50.0, not 50.

noteBlocks.prompt: A ball is timed twice between the same two markers: 2.14 s and 2.08 s. What is the mean time, in s?
noteBlocks.explain: Add the two timings, then divide by 2, as in step 2 of See it: (2.14 + 2.08) ÷ 2 = 2.11 s.

twin.prompt: Two timings for a trolley between two light gates are 1.37 s and 1.45 s. What is the mean time, in s?
twin.explain: Sum in brackets, then divide by the number of readings, as step 2 of See it did: (1.37 + 1.45) ÷ 2 = 1.41 s.

noteBlocks.md: Accurate means close to the true value, and depends on the instrument and how it is used. Reliable means repeats agree, so a slip shows up and a mean can be trusted. Valid means the experiment tests what it claims, because only the independent variable changes. Each promise has its own fix.

noteBlocks.title: Why one fix cannot do another's job
noteBlocks.md: Repeating a hand timing that always starts late gives the same late time again: the mean is reliable and still inaccurate. Light gates remove the late start. Only keeping everything else the same makes the test valid.

noteBlocks.stem: A student times a ball down a runway at five heights. Say which promise each part of her method keeps.

steps.working: She times each height three times and uses the mean
steps.decision: Repeats that agree: reliable. An odd timing stands out against the others.

steps.working: Light gates at the two markers start and stop the timing
steps.decision: No reaction time in the reading, so each time is closer to the true one: accurate.

steps.working: The same ball, released from the same point, with the markers the same distance apart
steps.decision: Only the height changes: valid.

steps.working: Not accuracy: three hand timings that agree
steps.decision: They could all start late by the same amount. Agreement proves reliability, nothing more.

noteBlocks.prompt: A student times a ball down a runway with a hand-held stopwatch. Which change would make each timing more accurate?
options: Use light gates at the markers
Use the same ball every time
Plot the results on a graph
noteBlocks.answer: Use light gates at the markers
noteBlocks.explain: Accuracy is closeness to the true value, which the instrument decides, as step 2 of See it showed: light gates take out the reaction time of a hand timing. More repeats make the mean reliable; the same ball keeps the test valid.

twin.prompt: In the same runway experiment, which change would make the experiment more valid?
options: Release the ball from the same point at every height
Use light gates at the markers
twin.answer: Release the ball from the same point at every height
twin.explain: Validity needs only the independent variable to change, as step 3 of See it kept the ball, release point and distance fixed.

optionNotes.option: Use light gates at the markers
optionNotes.why: That makes each timing more accurate; the test is only fair if nothing but the height changes.
Repeats make the results reliable, not the test valid.
More repeats make the mean reliable, but a late start is repeated five times too.

optionNotes.option: Use the same ball every time
optionNotes.why: That keeps the test valid by changing only the height; it does nothing to how close each time is.

optionNotes.option: Plot the results on a graph
optionNotes.why: A graph shows the pattern of the readings; it cannot make any one of them closer to the truth.

noteBlocks.text: Find the anomaly, leave it out, average

noteBlocks.md: An anomalous result does not fit the pattern of the others. Compare each reading with the rest, circle the odd one, repeat it if you can, and leave it out of the mean. Put brackets round the sum of the readings you keep, and divide by how many you kept, not how many you took.

noteBlocks.stem: Three timings for one height of the runway: 2.46 s, 2.52 s, 3.10 s. Find the mean.

steps.working: 3.10 s is far from the other two, which agree to within 0.06 s
steps.decision: Compare each reading with the rest: the odd one out does not fit.

steps.working: Leave 3.10 s out: circle it, and repeat that timing if you can
steps.decision: A late stop or a mis-read would drag the mean away from the truth.
Divide by the two readings kept, not the three taken.
It is above both good readings; a mean that matches none of them is the sign an anomaly was kept.

noteBlocks.prompt: Four readings of the focal length of one lens are 148 mm, 151 mm, 184 mm, 149 mm. Which reading is anomalous?
noteBlocks.explain: Compare each reading with the rest, as step 1 of See it did: three agree to within 3 mm and 184 mm is over 30 mm away, so it is left out before the mean is taken.

twin.prompt: Four timings for one run are 213 ms, 209 ms, 211 ms, 168 ms. Which reading is anomalous?
twin.explain: Three readings agree to within 4 ms; 168 ms is over 40 ms from them, so it does not fit, the step 1 test of See it.

optionNotes.why: It is within 4 ms of 209 ms and 211 ms, so it fits the pattern.
It is within 4 ms of 213 ms and 211 ms, so it fits the pattern.
It is within 2 ms of 213 ms and 209 ms, so it fits the pattern.
It is within 3 mm of 151 mm and 149 mm, so it fits the pattern.
It is within 3 mm of 148 mm and 149 mm, so it fits the pattern.
It is within 2 mm of 148 mm and 151 mm, so it fits the pattern.

noteBlocks.md: Some columns are worked out from others. The extension of a spring is its length minus its unstretched length, never the length itself. A rate is 1 ÷ time. A percentage change is the change ÷ the starting value × 100. Give each worked value to the places of the readings, or to the places asked for.

noteBlocks.stem: A spring is 12.0 cm long unstretched. With weights added, its lengths are 14.5 cm, 17.0 cm, 19.5 cm. Complete the extension column.

steps.decision: Extension = stretched length − unstretched length: subtract, every row.
Keep the readings' one decimal place: 5.0, not 5.
Each extension grows by the same amount for each equal weight added.

noteBlocks.prompt: A spring is 8.6 cm long unstretched and 13.4 cm long with a weight hanging on it. What is its extension, in cm?
noteBlocks.explain: Subtract the unstretched length from the stretched one, as step 1 of See it did: 13.4 − 8.6 = 4.8 cm. The stretched length on its own is not the extension.

twin.prompt: A spring 15.2 cm long unstretched is 21.0 cm long when a weight hangs on it. What is its extension, in cm?
twin.explain: Stretched length − unstretched length, as in step 1 of See it: 21.0 − 15.2 = 5.8 cm.

noteBlocks.text: Choose the scale, label the axes

noteBlocks.md: Use a linear scale that covers at least half the grid on each axis, in easy steps such as 1, 2, 5 or 10 to a large square. The independent variable goes across unless the question says otherwise. Label each axis with its column heading, quantity / unit, such as Time / s.

noteBlocks.stem: A graph of force against extension for a spring is a straight line through (0, 0), (2.0 cm, 0.5 N) and (12.0 cm, 3.0 N). Find the gradient, its unit and its meaning.

steps.decision: Two points far apart on the line, read from the line itself, give the most accurate gradient.
Rise ÷ run: the change up the side over the change across.

steps.working: Unit: N/cm
steps.decision: The y-axis unit per the x-axis unit.

steps.working: Meaning: the spring constant, k
steps.decision: F = ke, so force ÷ extension is k: the force needed for each centimetre of stretch.

noteBlocks.prompt: A graph has voltage / V up the side and current / A across. What is the unit of its gradient?
noteBlocks.explain: A gradient's unit is the y unit per the x unit, as step 3 of See it gave N/cm: here volts per amp, which is the ohm, Ω.

twin.prompt: A graph has resistance / Ω up the side and length / cm across. What is the unit of its gradient?
twin.explain: The y unit per the x unit, as in step 3 of See it: ohms per centimetre.

optionNotes.why: That is the y-axis unit alone; divide it by the x unit.
The units are there, but upside down: y over x, not x over y.
That is the y-axis unit alone; the gradient is a y unit per x unit.
That is the x unit over the y unit: the right units, upside down.
A gradient divides, so its unit is one unit per another, never a product.

noteBlocks.text: Why the gradient is the constant

noteBlocks.md: A straight line through the origin has the equation y = mx, where m is its gradient. Hooke's law, F = ke, has the same shape: with force up the side and extension across, the gradient is k. In the same way V = IR, with voltage up the side and current across, has gradient R.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that the gradient of a graph of force (up the side) against extension (across) for a spring is its spring constant, k.

steps.working: Hooke's law: F = ke, up to the limit of proportionality
steps.decision: The law is what makes the line straight and through the origin.

steps.working: A straight line through the origin: y = mx, gradient m
steps.decision: Any direct proportion plots this way.

steps.working: Match them: y is F, x is e, so m = k
steps.decision: The gradient takes the place of the constant.

steps.working: If the axes are swapped, extension up the side, the gradient is 1 ÷ k
steps.decision: Check which quantity is up the side before you use a gradient.

noteBlocks.prompt: A graph of extension (up the side, in cm) against force (across, in N) for a spring is a straight line through the origin with gradient 5 cm/N. What is the spring constant, in N/cm?
noteBlocks.explain: With extension up the side the gradient is e ÷ F, which is 1 ÷ k, as step 4 of See it showed. So k = 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 N/cm.

twin.prompt: A graph of current (up the side, in A) against voltage (across, in V) for a resistor is a straight line through the origin with gradient 0.125 A/V. What is its resistance, in Ω?
twin.explain: Current against voltage has gradient I ÷ V, which is 1 ÷ R, the swapped-axes case of step 4 of See it: R = 1 ÷ 0.125 = 8 Ω.

noteBlocks.md: **The axes are set for you.** Some questions put a quantity up the side that you might expect across, such as voltage against current or the angle of incidence. Plot as the question says, not as habit says.
**Part of the work is done.** "One point has been plotted for you" or "draw a curve starting at (0, 0)": use the given point, and start the curve where you are told.
**Places and forms.** A rate = 1 ÷ time to 4 decimal places keeps its last zero and is not written in standard form; a speed to 1 decimal place is 41.3, not 41.25.
**Mixed units.** A time written as 1 min 25 s is 85 s before it goes into a mean or a rate.

noteBlocks.stem: A cross under a flask disappears after 37 s. Work out the rate = 1 ÷ time, in s⁻¹, to 4 decimal places.

steps.decision: Keep every digit on the calculator until the last step.

steps.working: Rate = 0.0270 s⁻¹
steps.decision: The fourth place is a zero that must be written; standard form is not what was asked.

noteBlocks.prompt: A reaction takes 64 s. Which answer gives the rate = 1 ÷ time to 4 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: 1 ÷ 64 = 0.015625, and to 4 decimal places that is 0.0156, as step 2 of See it rounded 1 ÷ 37. Fewer places, more places or standard form each lose the mark.

twin.prompt: A time is recorded as 2 min 08 s. What is it in seconds?
twin.explain: Change minutes to seconds before using the time: 2 × 60 + 8 = 128 s. A time in mixed units cannot go into a rate as written.

optionNotes.why: That reads the minutes as hundreds of seconds; a minute is 60 s.
A clock time is not a decimal: 2 min 08 s is not 2.08 of anything.
The 08 is whole seconds to add, not a decimal of a second.
That is 3 decimal places; the question asks for 4.
The value is right, but standard form is not the 4 decimal places asked for.
Every digit the calculator shows, not rounded to 4 places.

noteBlocks.md: A Booklet B graph question often runs as one chain: plot the points, find the gradient with its unit, then say what the gradient means. Each step leans on the one before, so a well-drawn line makes the gradient easy to read.

noteBlocks.md:
Record readings to the stated places and take a mean with the anomaly left out.
Work out a new column: an extension by subtracting, a rate as 1 ÷ time.
Choose a linear scale, label the axes quantity / unit, and draw the right line.
Read a total from the level part of a curve, and a gradient with its unit and meaning.

A graph question is usually worth five marks: the scale, the label, the points and the line. A gradient earns its working, its value and its unit, and sometimes its meaning. Stuck? Find the anomaly first, then read each value from your line, never from the table.

A student hangs weights on a spring whose unstretched length is 7.5 cm.
Force / N: 1.2, 2.4, 3.6, 4.8
Length / cm: 9.5, 11.5, 13.5, 15.5
Find the extension for the 4.8 N weight. A graph of force (up the side) against extension (across) is a straight line through the origin. Use it to find the spring constant, give its unit and say what it means. [6]

steps.working: Extension = 15.5 − 7.5 = 8.0 cm
steps.decision: Subtract the unstretched length: the length itself is not the extension.

steps.working: Two points far apart on the line: (0, 0) and (8.0 cm, 4.8 N), so the rise is 4.8 N
steps.decision: A large triangle, from points on the line itself.

steps.working: Gradient = 4.8 ÷ 8.0 = 0.6
steps.decision: Rise ÷ run.

options: F = ke, so force ÷ extension is k, and that is what the gradient measures
The gradient of any spring graph is 1
The gradient is the extension for each newton
whyMenu.explain: With force up the side and extension across, rise ÷ run is F ÷ e, which Hooke's law says is k. Swap the axes and the gradient would be 1 ÷ k.

steps.working: Unit: N/cm
steps.decision: The y-axis unit per the x-axis unit.

steps.working: k = 0.6 N/cm: the force needed to stretch the spring by 1 cm
steps.decision: Say what the number stands for.

options.text: the force needed for each centimetre of extension
options.feedback: Newtons per centimetre: force for each cm of stretch.
That is 1 ÷ k, the axes read the other way round.
The gradient is about how the force changes with the extension, not the length.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: k = 0.6 N/cm, the force for each centimetre of extension

The graph of voltage (up the side) against current (across) is a straight line through the origin. Calculate the gradient of the line and state its unit. [4]

steps.working: Two points far apart on the line: (0, 0) and (0.50 A, 5.5 V). Rise = 5.5 V
steps.decision: Gradient = rise ÷ run: the equation first, from points on the line.

steps.working: Run = 0.50 A
steps.decision: The run is the change across, in amps.

steps.working: Gradient = 5.5 ÷ 0.50 = 11
steps.decision: Rise ÷ run.

options: V = IR, so voltage ÷ current is the resistance: the gradient of this graph
The gradient is the current for each volt
The gradient is always the largest voltage
whyMenu.explain: With voltage up the side and current across, rise ÷ run is V ÷ I, the resistance. A straight line through the origin means the resistance stays the same.

steps.working: Unit: Ω (volts per amp)
steps.decision: The y unit per the x unit: V/A, which is the ohm.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Four readings of the focal length of a lens are 247 mm, 253 mm, 250 mm, 206 mm. Calculate the most reliable value of the focal length. [2]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: 206 mm is far from the other three, which agree to within 6 mm, so it is anomalous and must be left out. The mean of the other three is (247 + 253 + 250) ÷ 3 = 250 mm.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks: the anomaly is in the mean, so neither the sum nor the value earns. Summer 2024 Booklet B examiners saw a substantial number lose both marks this way.

findTheMistake.stem:
Sam is asked: 'Gas volumes read every 20 s are 0, 21, 33, 39, 41, 42, 42 cm³. What is the total volume of gas given off? [1]'
His answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Each reading is the total volume so far, not a new amount, so adding them counts the same gas again and again. The readings level off at 42 cm³, and that is the total.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks. Summer 2025 Booklet B examiners saw many add up every reading in the table.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'A graph of resistance / Ω against length / m for a wire is a straight line through the origin. Use the triangle shown (rise 6.4 Ω, run 0.40 m) to find the gradient, and give its unit. [4]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The working and the value are right. A gradient's unit is the y-axis unit per the x-axis unit, so here it is ohms per metre, Ω/m, not the y unit alone.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks of four: only the unit's mark is lost. Summer 2025 Booklet B examiners found the gradient's unit defeated a surprising number.

findings.asked: Plot a volume-time graph and read the total volume of gas from it.
findings.wentWrong: The x-axis label was the usual lost mark; many read the total by adding every value in the table instead of from the flat part of the curve.
findings.rule: Both axes labelled with quantity and unit; totals come from the plateau.

findings.asked: Calculate an average from repeated readings, one of which is anomalous.
findings.wentWrong: A substantial number included the anomalous reading in the average and lost both marks.
findings.rule: Circle the anomaly, leave it out, then average.

findings.asked: Plot a graph from circuit readings.
findings.wentWrong: Well plotted, but a small minority chose a non-linear scale.
findings.rule: Equal distances on an axis mean equal steps in the quantity.

findings.asked: Plot a current-voltage graph for a lamp.
findings.wentWrong: Axis labels were missed by a few, unsuitable scales by the least able, and some ruled straight lines from point to point instead of drawing a curve.
findings.rule: Best-fit line or smooth curve - never dot-to-dot.

findings.asked: Measure a drawn cell and its nucleus against a scale, then give the ratio of the two diameters.
findings.wentWrong: The measuring was mostly right, but fewer gave the ratio correctly: many wrote it the wrong way round.
findings.rule: Write a ratio in the order the question names the two quantities.

findings.asked: Plot resistance against length of wire, find the gradient and its unit.
findings.wentWrong: The graph was excellent apart from the odd missing label or unit; the gradient was calculated, but its unit defeated a surprising number.
findings.rule: Gradient unit = y-axis unit per x-axis unit (ohms per cm).

insight.ruleToRemember: Label both axes with quantity and unit (matching the table headings), choose linear scales that use most of the grid, plot accurately, then draw a straight line or smooth curve of best fit - never join the dots. Spot and exclude anomalies before averaging, read values from the line, give ratios in the order asked, and give a gradient its unit.
insight.aStarSignal: A graph that needs no correction, an anomaly handled and explained, and a gradient with its unit and physical meaning.
